## Task 4 

This is all about learning about packages, how to install and how to load up the functions. Below is the code to install a function, but I used the chunk setting `#| eval: false` to stop it from evaluating. We don't want that. We only want to run that code once when we first install the packages.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("gapminder")
```

As I want to use these packages today I now load in my libraries. 

```{r}
#| label: packages 
#| echo: true

library("tidyverse")
library("gapminder")
```

We loaded the tidyverse package as we will use that a lot this semester. It contains lots of helpful functions for data analysis and data visualisation. 

We loaded the gapminder package as this package contains data, also called gapminder, that we are planning on using. 

Let's take a quick look at that data. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
gapminder
```

In R console I can look at my data with the `View()` function. 

In my Quarto I might want to take a quick look at the first few rows instead of printing everything out. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
head(gapminder, 2)
```

There are other options for looking at your data. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
glimpse(gapminder)
```

Let's try saving this data out and then reading it back in again. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
write_csv(gapminder, "gapminder.csv")
gapminder_csv <- read_csv("gapminder.csv")
glimpse(gapminder_csv)
all(gapminder == gapminder_csv)
```

## Task 5 

How else can we look at our data. Well we can find out how many rows and columns it has

```{r}
#| echo: true
num_rows = nrow(gapminder)
num_cols = ncol(gapminder)
```

Here I have `{r} num_rows` rows and `{r} num_cols` columns.

And the function `dim()` gives you the dimensions of your data, so the rows and the columns.

So let's check that we get the same values:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
dim(gapminder)
```

1. Create a variable `pop`

```{r}
pop <- gapminder$pop
length(pop)
nrow(gapminder)
```
2. Take a look at life expectancy 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
mean_lifeExp <- round(mean(gapminder$lifeExp))
min_lifeExp <- round(min(gapminder$lifeExp))
max_lifeExp <- round(max(gapminder$lifeExp))
```

The average life expectancy is `{r} mean_lifeExp` but the range is `{r} min_lifeExp` to `{r} max_lifeExp`.

3. Calculate the population in millions

```{r}
pop_in_millions <- pop/1000000
max(pop_in_millions)
```

The largest population recorded in this data set is `{r} 1318` million people and that is for the country of China in 2007.

4. Taking a look at the range now

```{r}
range(gapminder$gdpPercap)
range(log10(gapminder$gdpPercap))
```
We are going to see later why transforming our data can sometimes help communication our messages. A common way to transform our data is using the base 10 log or the exponential.

5. Let's break some stuff

This example shows that our variable names in R are case sensitive! If we get the name wrong our file won't render. (Here I use `eval: false` to show you the chunk and ensure the Quarto renders.)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
GAPMINDER
```

Same issue here! But in this example it just returns an empty column instead and gives a warning. Lucky! Good reason to check our warning messages.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
gapminder$LifeExp
```

## Task 6 

Now let's produce a plot 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

plot <- ggplot(data = gapminder) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, colour = country)) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
plot
```

```
